blocks.text: Lest anyone think this manner of speaking peculiar to the poets, it also occurs in Columella, book 10, chapter 3: The whole nation of an entire hive is consumed. And in chapter 9: Whole nations (of bees) are consumed by civil war. And in chapter 10, of the king of the bees whose wings have been removed: He does not even allow the people of his own dominion to roam farther. And in chapter 13: Two peoples must be joined. And of the drones, in chapter 15: Nor is the nation to be destroyed to the point of extermination. Similar is what Aelian, book 6 of the History, chapter 19, called τὸ τεττίγων φῦλον [to tettigōn phylon], the nation of cicadas. For so he had written, not φῶλον [phōlon], a meaningless word, which [III, 295] our editions have. Moreover, the Arabic lexicographers Giauhari and Alcamus note that in Arabic too أمة [umma] umma, nation, is said of any animal. So in the celebrated saying of the pseudo-prophet about the animals, which we cited above ^{b)}: خلق الله الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد [khalaqa Allāh alf umma minhā sittumiʾa fī al-baḥr wa-arbaʿumiʾa fī al-barr wa-inna awwal halāk hādhihi al-umam al-jarād] God created a thousand nations of animals (so it reads word for word), six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land. And the first plague of these nations is the locust. Why then should Joel not have called the locusts here גוי, a nation, and עם, a people, in chapter 2, verse 2?

To them are assigned the teeth and molars of lions, as in Apoc. IX, 8. Ὀδόντες αὐτῶν ὡς λεόντων ἦσαν [Odontes autōn hōs leontōn ēsan], Their teeth were as those of lions, that is, hard, strong, sharp. Accordingly Pliny says of locusts: Gnawing everything with their bite, even the doors of houses. This strength is truly astonishing in so paltry a little creature. So not without reason does Jerome exclaim at these words: What is stronger than locusts, which human industry cannot resist? And Cyril: Ἄμαχον τὸ χρῆμά ἐστι, καὶ ἀκαταγώνιστος κομιδῆ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ ἔφοδος, ἱκανή τε ἄρδην ἀπολέσαι τὰ ἐν ἀγροῖς. [Amachon to chrēma esti, kai akatagōnistos komidē tōn toioutōn hē ephodos, hikanē te ardēn apolesai ta en agrois.] [col. 469] The thing is invincible; their onset is utterly irresistible and fully capable of destroying the wealth of the countryside. What they have bitten off the Arabs call تاشر [tāshur], that is, toothed like a saw. For اشر [ashara] means to cut with a saw ^{(1)}.

Verse 7: He has laid my vine waste, and my fig tree broken. He has stripped it bare and cast it away; its branches are made white.] He says vine and fig tree, because bruchi and locusts are harmful to both. Accordingly, to keep bruchi away from vines, Didymus prescribes this in book 10 of the Geoponica: Περὶ τὸ στέλεχος τῆς ἀμπέλου παρὰ τὴν ῥίζαν, τρεῖς κόκκους σινήπεως χῶσον· φυτευόμενα γὰρ ταῦτα τῇ ὀσμῇ τὸν βροῦχον ἀναιρεῖ. [Peri to stelechos tēs ampelou para tēn rhizan, treis kokkous sinēpeōs chōson; phyteuomena gar tauta tē osmē ton brouchon anairei.] Bury three grains of mustard around the trunk of the vine at the root: for when planted they kill the bruchus by their smell. And of fig trees Pliny, book 17, chapter 25: In Boeotia fig trees gnawed by locusts sprouted again. This is taken from these words of Theophrastus, book 2 of the History, chapter 4: Ἐν δὲ τῇ Βοιωτίᾳ καταβρωθέντων τῶν ἔργων ὑπὸ τῶν ἀττελέβων πάλιν ἀνεβλάστησε. [En de tē Boiōtia katabrōthentōn tōn ergōn hypo tōn attelebōn palin aneblastēse.] Therefore instead of τῶν ἔργων [tōn ergōn] one should read τῶν ἐρίνων [tōn erinōn]. For ἔρινα [erina] are wild figs, or any unripe figs, as [III, 296] in Alexis in Athenaeus. I render the Hebrew לקצפה into breaking, with the Greeks, who here have εἰς κλασμὸν [eis klasmon] or συγκλασμόν [synklasmon] ^{(2)}. This rendering of a word otherwise unusual is confirmed from Arabic usage. For in Arabic قصف [qaṣafa] means to break, and القصيف [al-qaṣīf] is a broken branch of a tree. So Giauhari and Ibno-maruph. This is very much to the point, provided it is referred to the topmost branches of trees, on which locusts feed. Hence some think they are called ἀκρίδες [akrides], παρὰ τὸ ἄκρας τῶν ἀσταχύων καὶ τῶν φυτῶν νέμεσθαι [para to akras tōn astachyōn kai tōn phytōn nemesthai]. For Jerome קצפה is decortication. Accordingly he has here, He has stripped the bark from my fig tree. And more than once he writes that trees are stripped of bark by locusts. So on Hosea chapter 13: The locust is so harmful that it strips the bark even from trees and vines. And on Joel: the Jews think that in the days of Joel so innumerable a multitude of locusts came that they did not spare even the bark and branches of the vines and trees. And below: Locusts lay everything waste to such a degree that they gnaw away the bark of trees. The Chaldee, who rendered the word קצפה quite differently, nevertheless concluded that trees are stripped of bark by locusts from what follows about the fig tree, חשף חשפה, stripping he has stripped it, which he interprets thus: מקלף קלף, barking he has barked it. But for a tree to be said to be stripped, it is not necessary that its bark be removed. It suffices that the leaves and fruit, or flowers, be taken away. Hence the old Poet in the Description of the Four Seasons of the Year:
Winter strips the grove of its leaves, and the rivers grow stiff.
